title: DHS Proposes $103,265 Fee on Every H-1B Cap Petition in Sweeping Rulemaking
excerpt: DHS says the fee would recover $8.8 billion a year in federal immigration costs. Unlike the struck-down $100,000 order, it would apply even to F-1 students changing status inside the U.S.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $103,265 fee on every H-1B cap-subject petition, on top of all existing filing fees, estimating it would collect $8.8 billion a year.
  • The fee would apply to all 85,000 annual cap petitions — including the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption and F-1 students changing status inside the U.S. — but not to cap-exempt petitions from universities and nonprofit research organizations.
  • The rule is legally distinct from the 2025 executive-order $100,000 H-1B fee, which a federal court vacated in June 2026 and which only applied to consular processing abroad.
  • If finalized, the fee would apply prospectively to fiscal year 2028 petitions (calendar year 2027), with significant legal challenges expected.

The Department of Homeland Security is proposing to charge employers $103,265 for every H-1B petition filed under the annual cap — a fee that would dwarf all existing immigration filing costs and fundamentally change the economics of hiring foreign specialty workers. The proposal, published as a notice of proposed rulemaking on August 25, 2026, would apply to all cap-subject petitions, including those under the advanced-degree exemption, and would be paid at the time of filing in addition to all other applicable fees.

According to the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services announcement dated August 24, the proposed fee is designed to recover a portion of the federal government's costs for administering the lawful immigration system — covering adjudication, fraud detection, national security vetting, systems modernization, records operations, immigration court operations, consular visa processing, labor standards enforcement, and interagency coordination. DHS estimates the fee would generate approximately $8.8 billion annually, based on a projected annual volume of 85,000 H-1B cap-subject petitions.

Breaking with how USCIS fees have worked

Historically, USCIS fee rules recovered only the agency's own costs. This proposal adopts a novel interagency cost-recovery approach: the fee would recover roughly $8.78 billion in identified costs spread across six federal agencies, including USCIS, the Department of Labor, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of State, Customs and Border Protection, and the Justice Department's Executive Office for Immigration Review. About 64 percent of the costs captured in the fee are incurred outside of USCIS, according to the rulemaking notice.

"The proposed H-1B fee is intended to recover the costs incurred across the federal government to adjudicate, vet, and support lawful immigration programs that otherwise must be funded by taxpayers."

— Zach Kahler, USCIS spokesperson

Divided among the 85,000 projected cap-subject petitions, those costs work out to approximately $103,265 per petition. The proposed rule states that cap-subject H-1B employers are best suited to bear these costs rather than spreading them across all immigration applicants and petitioners.

Not the same as the $100,000 fee

The new proposal is legally distinct from the $100,000 H-1B payment imposed by presidential proclamation in September 2025. That earlier fee, issued under Proclamation 10973 as a restriction on entry, applied only to H-1B workers seeking status through consular processing abroad — sparing those who changed to H-1B status inside the United States, most commonly international students. A federal district court in Massachusetts vacated the implementing guidance on June 8, 2026, and the administration's appeal to the First Circuit Court of Appeals remains pending.

The proposed rulemaking fee reaches further. It would apply to all 85,000 initial cap petitions — the 65,000 regular-cap slots plus the 20,000 advanced-degree exemptions — regardless of whether the beneficiary is abroad or already in the United States and seeking a change of status. An F-1 student switching to H-1B without leaving the country would face the fee, as would employers of every size, including nonprofits, so long as the petition is cap-subject.

Who is exempt — and what it means for Indian professionals

The fee would not apply to H-1B petitions not subject to the cap: those filed by institutions of higher education, nonprofit research organizations, governmental research organizations, and affiliated nonprofits. But the vast majority of private-sector employers — including the technology, health care, engineering, and finance companies that sponsor most H-1B workers — file cap-subject petitions, and for many of them the proposed fee would sit atop existing filing costs of roughly $6,300 per petition before premium processing.

Indian nationals receive the largest share of H-1B visas each year. If the rule takes effect, employers weighing whether to sponsor a foreign hire — or to extend an offer to an Indian graduate on OPT — would face a six-figure government cost before any salary is paid, which could cool demand for H-1B hiring or push recruiting toward cap-exempt institutions.

What's next

The rule is still a proposal, and the notice-and-comment process means employers, industry groups, and immigration advocates will now file objections before anything is finalized. Significant legal challenges are widely anticipated, particularly given the novel interagency cost-recovery theory and the court's earlier ruling that the 2025 fee amounted to an unlawful tax. If the rule survives, it would apply prospectively to H-1B cap petitions for fiscal year 2028 — filed in calendar year 2027. Meanwhile, the 2025 proclamation's $100,000 payment, currently vacated, is set to expire on September 21, 2026, one year after its issuance, unless extended.
